        "statement": "Let $I\\subseteq\\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two elements ([[def-interval]]), let $\\theta_0\\in I$, and let $f:I\\to\\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on $I$ in the sense that $f$ is differentiable at every point of $I$ and $f'$ is continuous on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]). Assume $f(\\theta_0)=0$ and that $f'(\\theta)\\ge m>0$ for every $\\theta\\in I$. Let a recorded scalar $\\hat y\\in\\mathbb R$ satisfy $|\\hat y|\\le s$ with $s\\ge0$ ([[def-abs-value]]), and let a separately specified calibration-error model bound be $|y-\\hat y|\\le\\delta$ with $\\delta\\ge0$ for a value $y$ assigned to the same quantity. If a model requires $y=f(\\theta)$ for some $\\theta\\in I$, then every $\\theta\\in I$ compatible with those two simultaneous bounds satisfies $$|\\theta-\\theta_0|\\le\\frac{s+\\delta}{m};$$ equivalently, if a proposed $\\theta$ violates this bound, then the specified model-plus-error-bound pair is incompatible with the premises. The conclusion is a deterministic conditional statement about the stated bounds; it is not a sampling law, a statistical inference, or a claim about the historical reports of the causal-response page.",
        "strategy": "The triangle inequality for the absolute value ([[lem-of-triangle-inequality]], [[def-abs-value]]) gives $|y|\\le|\\hat y|+|y-\\hat y|\\le s+\\delta$. For $\\theta\\ne\\theta_0$ apply the mean value theorem ([[cor-mean-value-theorem]]) to $f$ on the closed interval with endpoints $\\theta$ and $\\theta_0$ (an interval contained in $I$ by order convexity, [[def-interval]]): there is $\\xi$ strictly between them with $f(\\theta)-f(\\theta_0)=f'(\\xi)(\\theta-\\theta_0)$, hence $|f(\\theta)|\\ge m|\\theta-\\theta_0|$ because $f(\\theta_0)=0$ and $f'\\ge m>0$. Combining $|f(\\theta)|=|y|\\le s+\\delta$ with the lower bound and dividing by $m>0$ gives the stated bound; $\\theta=\\theta_0$ is immediate. Differentiability of $f$ everywhere and continuity of $f'$ on $I$ ([[def-derivative]], [[def-continuity-real]]) are used to make $f$ continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on its interior, exactly the mean-value hypotheses.         "statement": "For $z\\in[-1,1]$ define the real polynomial $P_l(z)=\\pi^{-1}\\int_0^\\pi\\bigl[z+i\\sqrt{1-z^2}\\,\\cos\\theta\\bigr]^l\\,d\\theta$, $l\\in\\mathbb N_0$. Then $P_l$ is a real polynomial of degree at most $l$ with $|P_l(z)|\\le1$ on $[-1,1]$, $P_l(1)=1$, and for $|q|<1$ the series $\\sum_{l\\ge0}q^lP_l(z)$ converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-1,1]$ with $$(1-2qz+q^2)^{-1/2}=\\sum_{l=0}^{\\infty}q^lP_l(z),$$ where the branch is the analytic square root equal to $1$ at $q=0$ ([[def-series-of-real-functions]], [[thm-weierstrass-m-test-for-function-series]]). Consequently, for $r>|y|$ with $n=x/|x|$ and $N\\in\\mathbb N_0$, $\\bigl|\\,|x-y|^{-1}-\\sum_{l=0}^{N}|y|^l|x|^{-l-1}P_l(n\\cdot y/|y|)\\bigr|\\le|y|^{N+1}|x|^{-N-2}(1-|y|/|x|)^{-1}$, uniformly on $|y|\\le a<r$ (with $y=0$ interpreted by the zero higher terms), and after integrating against an $L^1$ source the corresponding multipole expansion converges with that error times its $L^1$ norm. For the integrated $L^1$-source and every-spatial-derivative assertions, assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) through the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate interfaces. On an observation compact set disjoint from $\\overline{B_a(0)}$ every fixed spatial derivative series converges uniformly, uniformly also over $|y|\\le a$, by harmonicity of the coefficient terms and [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]]. The initial finite-Riemann polynomial/generating assertions are choice-free. This lemma supplies the convergent zonal kernel; it does not by itself prove a spherical $L^2$ basis or boundary convergence.",

No holomorphy in z at the endpoints is asserted.\n\nFor real $a>|b|$ the tangent substitution gives $I(a,b)=\\int_0^\\pi(a+b\\cos\\theta)^{-1}d\\theta=\\pi/\\sqrt{a^2-b^2}$ by [[thm-substitution]] and [[thm-principal-inverse-tangent-calculus]]. Near $(a,b)=(1,0)$ the rational integrand and its first parameter derivatives are uniformly bounded on the compact theta interval, so uniform difference quotients through the finite Riemann integral give holomorphy in each parameter separately. The corresponding degree-l solid polynomial in y is harmonic in y by the same argument, using $\\Delta_y|x-ty|^{-1}=0$ for all sufficiently small real t. This also supplies the solid-harmonic coefficient used by the later addition lemma without a cyclic dependence.\n\nThe empty observation compact has a vacuous uniform-convergence claim. Otherwise fix a nonempty compact observation set K with inf_K|x|>a. Choose a positive delta and a bounded closed neighbourhood Kplus of K with every closed delta-ball centred on K contained in Kplus and inf_Kplus|x|>a. The geometric kernel estimate gives a uniform tail bound E_N tending to zero on Kplus times the whole closed source ball |y|<=a. Harmonic partial-sum differences v satisfy the exact [[thm-interior-derivative-estimates-for-harmonic-functions]] bound $|D^\\alpha v(x)|\\le C_{3,\\alpha}\\delta^{-3-|\\alpha|}\\int_{B_\\delta(x)}|v|\\le C_{3,\\alpha}\\delta^{-3-|\\alpha|}|B_\\delta|\\sup_{Kplus}|v|$. Thus every spatial derivative is uniformly Cauchy on K, uniformly in y. Uniform derivative limits are identified inductively along short coordinate segments by [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]], so they are exactly the derivatives of the kernel. Against a compact $L^1$ density, the same bound times |rho| gives an integrable envelope and multiplies each tail by ||rho||1 using [[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]. Countable Choice enters only the Lebesgue and harmonic-estimate branches; the initial finite polynomial and scalar generating argument uses no Choice. No multivariable complex Cauchy estimate is invoked. For an actual L1 source choose its representative zero outside the closed source ball. On each small open observation-coordinate interval inside Kplus, every kernel derivative is smooth on the fixed compact source ball and has a uniform finite bound C_alpha; the next derivative integrand is bounded by C_alpha times |rho|, an integrable majorant.         "statement": "Let $c>0$, $0\\le v_*<c$, and $z:\\mathbb R\\to\\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ with $|z'(s)|\\le v_*$ for all $s$. For every $(x,t)\\in\\mathbb R^3\\times\\mathbb R$ there is exactly one real root $s=s(x,t)$ of $t-s=|x-z(s)|/c$, and $s\\le t$. Equality holds exactly when $x=z(t)$. Thus on the open off-instantaneous-worldline domain $D=\\{(x,t):x\\ne z(t)\\}$ one has $s<t$, $r=|x-z(s)|=c(t-s)>0$, and the root is $C^1$. With $n=(x-z(s))/r$, $\\beta=z'(s)/c$, and $\\kappa=1-n\\cdot\\beta$, its derivatives are $\\partial_t s=1/\\kappa$ and $\\nabla_xs=-n/(c\\kappa)$, where $1-v_*/c\\le\\kappa\\le1+v_*/c$. If $z$ is $C^k$, for an integer $k\\ge1$, the root is $C^k$ on $D$; in particular a $C^3$ trajectory gives a $C^3$ root. A smooth trajectory gives a smooth root. No higher regularity follows from a merely $C^1$ trajectory. These claims concern an all-time uniformly subluminal prescribed history; no finite-history or nonuniform-light-speed-limit assertion is made.",
        "strategy": "The ordinary vector FTC and integral triangle inequality give $|z(s_2)-z(s_1)|\\le v_*|s_2-s_1|$. For fixed $x$ put $g_x(s)=s+|x-z(s)|/c$. It is continuous and for $s_2>s_1$ satisfies $g_x(s_2)-g_x(s_1)\\ge(1-v_*/c)(s_2-s_1)>0$. Consequently $g_x(s)\\to\\pm\\infty$ as $s\\to\\pm\\infty$; IVT and strict monotonicity give a unique solution of $g_x(s)=t$. Since $g_x(s)\\ge s$, $s\\le t$, and equality is equivalent to $x=z(t)$. On $D$ the root has $r>0$. Continuity of $z$ makes $D$ open. Near any root on $D$, $F(x,t,s)=t-s-|x-z(s)|/c$ has precisely the regularity of $z$, because the Euclidean norm is smooth away from zero. Its $s$ derivative is $-\\kappa$, bounded away from zero. Apply the parametrized implicit-function theorem with its actual $C^1$ hypothesis first, or with $C^k$ when $z$ is $C^k$; global uniqueness glues these local maps. Differentiating $F=0$ gives the two stated formulas. Repeat for every finite $k$ in the smooth case. Do not infer $C^3$ from $C^1$, and do not exclude an observation point merely because the trajectory visits it at a different time. The exact non-improvement witness is a small uniformly subluminal $z(s)=(\\epsilon\\chi(s)|s|^{3/2},0,0)$ with smooth compact cutoff $\\chi=1$ near zero. At a distant positive axial point $L>\\sup|z|$, the retardation map is $g(s)=s+(L-\\epsilon\\chi(s)|s|^{3/2})/c$, $C^1$ but not $C^2$ at zero. A $C^2$ inverse near $t=L/c$, whose derivative is nonzero, would make $g$ $C^2$ by the inverse-function theorem, a contradiction."

This signed scalar rapidity statement does not identify a vector beta in R^3 with the scalar tanh r. For $k=1,2,3$ and $\\sigma\\in\\{+1,-1\\}$ use the relatively open patch $\\sigma x_k>r/(2\\sqrt3)$; these six patches cover because some $|x_k|\\ge r/\\sqrt3$. In rigid coordinates $(y,z)$ with $z=\\sigma x_k$, each patch lies on the positive graph $z=h(y)=\\sqrt{r^2-|y|^2}$. Around each point choose a graph cylinder small enough that $z>0$, $|y|<r$ and any other annulus boundary is absent. The sphere is exactly this graph, and the ball is exactly $z<h(y)$ there. The chain and power rules make $h$ smooth on $|y|<r$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]).         "statement": "Adopt post-sr-ideal-clocks-and-light and post-sr-inertial-covariance, and the SI conventions of def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions; let the inertial frames and charts x, x' with boost parameter v be as in lem-sr-boost-time-length-and-velocity-formulas. (ii) Length contraction. For a rod at rest in the frame x' of rest length L_0, with endpoints carried along the worldlines y_a, y_b of the lemma, the length assigned to it by the frame x on a simultaneity slice of x is L_0/gamma; symmetrically, a rod at rest in x has length L_0/gamma as measured by x'. Measured length here is defined by the stated protocol (events of the endpoints at equal time in the measuring frame); it is not the optical appearance of a moving rod, and no claim is made about a rod whose state of motion changes. (iii) Relativity of simultaneity. Two events simultaneous in x (equal x^0) with separation L in the boost direction generally fail to be simultaneous in x', with x'^0-difference -gamma (v/c) L; hence simultaneity is not an observer-independent relation. Each inertial frame's simultaneity is exactly the simultaneity relation of its time axis in the sense of def-sr-simultaneity-slice-and-rest-distance, operationally reproduced by its radar protocol as established in pthm-sr-radar-synchronization-of-inertial-observers. (iv) Velocity transformation.         "statement": "Let Omega be a nonempty open subset of A. (i) Flow box. For a smooth nowhere-zero one-form alpha on Omega let D := ker alpha be the hyperplane distribution D_p = {v in V : alpha_p(v) = 0}. Then D is integrable on Omega (through every point there passes a local hypersurface whose tangent space at each of its points is the corresponding D_p) if and only if alpha wedge d alpha = 0 on Omega. (iii) Rest distributions of observer congruences. Let n be an observer congruence on Omega, alpha := n-flat, and let theta, omega be its expansion and vorticity (definition of the congruence kinematics).         "strategy": "Fix one inertial affine chart, identifying U with an open subset of R^4, and write alpha=sum_i a_i dx^i. Closedness for a C^1 form means partial_i a_j=partial_j a_i. On any convex ball B contained in U, fix b in B and set phi(x)=integral_0^1 sum_i a_i(b+t(x-b))(x_i-b_i) dt. For x in B and sufficiently small h, the radial segments for x+h e_j lie in a compact subset of B. The parameter derivative of the integrand is continuous on that compact set. The one-variable FTC expresses its difference quotient as the average of that derivative along x+u h e_j; uniform continuity makes these averages converge uniformly in t. Hence taking the integral of the quotient gives partial_j phi(x)=integral_0^1 [a_j(b+t(x-b))+t sum_i (x_i-b_i) partial_j a_i(b+t(x-b))]dt. Closedness and the chain rule identify the integrand with d/dt[t a_j(b+t(x-b))], so FTC gives partial_j phi=a_j. These partial derivatives are continuous, hence phi is C^1; since all a_j are C^1, phi is C^2. Chain rule and FTC on each path piece give integral_gamma alpha=phi(gamma(1))-phi(gamma(0)) for every piecewise-C^1 path contained in B. Uniform continuity of H gives delta>0 such that domain distances less than delta imply image distances less than r/2. Choose a finite rectangular mesh with cell diameter less than delta. For each cell, its lower-left image vertex belongs to a half-radius ball; the entire cell image is therefore contained in the corresponding full-radius ball. Only finitely many ball assignments are made.         "statement": "(a) Preservation. Let x: I -> A be a C^2 future timelike worldline and let X,Y: I -> V be C^1 Fermi-Walker transported fields along x (def-sr-fermi-walker-transport). (b) Rindler wedge congruence. In an inertial chart (x^0,x,y,z) consider Phi(theta,rho,y,z) := (rho sinh theta, rho cosh theta, y, z) on R x (0,inf) x R^2, with theta in R and rho>0. (c) Rigid rotation, ambient nonintegrability and ring holonomy. Fix real Omega. In the inertial chart let U_Omega be the open timelike region r^2=(x^1)^2+(x^2)^2<c^2/Omega^2 when Omega!=0, and the whole chart when Omega=0. On this four-dimensional open set put K=partial_0+(Omega/c)(-x^2 partial_1+x^1 partial_2), gamma(r)=(1-Omega^2 r^2/c^2)^(-1/2), and n=gamma(r)K. This is a smooth future unit timelike Born-rigid congruence. If Omega!=0, its three-dimensional rest distribution in the ambient open set is nowhere integrable: its vorticity is nowhere zero and no ambient rest-simultaneity hypersurface exists locally.
